region: La Florida · San Bartolomé, Lanzarote, Canary Islands, Spain
title: Los Bermejos Diego Seco
about: Los Bermejos takes its name from the estate where it stands, at La Florida in San Bartolomé, at the foot of a volcano named after Juan Bello, one of the founding family. A new company revived the winery in 2001, and today it is owned and run by winemaker Ignacio Valdera. Lanzarote is the easternmost of the Canary Islands, about 125 km off the African coast, and between 1730 and 1736 an eruption buried the island under three to five metres of lava and ash. Valdera also buys grapes from growers who share his commitment to sustainable farming.

That volcanic crust is infertile, so each vine is planted in its own hoyo, a pit dug down through the ash to the old soil beneath and ringed with a low stone wall against the constant wind. The vines grow low to the ground, every task is done by hand, and yields are tiny, around 16 hectolitres per hectare. Diego is a white grape native to Lanzarote and La Palma, known for its high acidity and mineral character. Los Bermejos ferments it in stainless steel and leaves it on its lees in tank for three months.

Diego Seco is the dry, single-variety version of the grape; the winery also makes a dry Malvasía, a sweet Moscatel and reds from Listán Negro. Unoaked and bottled at 13.5% alcohol, it is all about the grape’s natural acidity and the mineral tension that comes from volcanic ground. The importer lists it as Diego Seco Ecológico (organic), though it notes that organic certification at Los Bermejos depends on the vintage.
facts: Dry, unoaked white, three months on lees
